themes.def: The sky as the upper world, father of the pair Heaven-and-Earth.
The pressed plant and the juice made from it, drunk by the gods and by the sacrificer; the substance, not the deity of the same name.
Fire as the ritual and natural phenomenon: the flame kindled on the altar and the burning that consumes, warms and carries. NOT the deity Agni, which is VG:DEVATA:AGNIH.
Goods and riches asked for from the gods, counted in cattle, horses, gold and heroes rather than in money.
The sacrificial rite itself, the act of worship offered to the gods with fire, speech and oblation.
Cows and cattle, the principal wealth of the corpus and the object of the raid that several central myths retell.
The act and occasion of pressing out the soma, the rite around which most of the Rigvedic liturgy is organised.
Speech as a power: the voice that carries the hymn and, in some hymns, a cosmic agent in her own right.
The chariot, the vehicle of gods and warriors and the standing image for a well-made hymn.
The waters as a plural collective: rivers, rain and the primeval flood, invoked as mothers and as healers.
The right ordering of the world, of the seasons and of the rite, which gods and men are said to follow rather than to legislate.
The people as a body: the clan, the tribe, the settled folk on whose behalf the rite is performed.
The aid a god is asked to bring, the single most frequent request in the corpus.
Physical force and overpowering vigour, the quality by which a god prevails.
The earth as the lower world and as the broad surface that bears living things.
The sun as the visible luminary that crosses the sky and measures the day.
The prize or booty won in a contest, and by metonymy the vigour that wins it.
The act of praising a god, and the composed praise-song as an offering in its own right.
Visionary thought, the poet's insight that produces the hymn rather than ordinary reasoning.
The bond of comradeship, invoked between the worshipper and the god as a claim rather than a sentiment.
What is poured or placed in the fire for the gods, considered as the offered material rather than as the rite.
The formulated sacred utterance and the power in it, before the word acquired its later Upanishadic sense.
The officiant who invokes and offers, named by office rather than as an individual.
Daybreak, and the recurring arrival of light that the hymns treat as a daily renewal of the world.
Light as such: the brightness a god makes, finds or gives, distinct from the body that emits it.
Rule: the king, his realm and the sovereign authority attributed equally to men and to Varuna.
The bolt, Indra's weapon, treated as a distinct object rather than as lightning.
A flowing river, named generically; the specific named rivers stay in the place layer rather than here.
Coming into being: birth, begetting and the generation of the world in the cosmogonic hymns.
Being well and getting through safely; the closing wish of a great many hymns.
Mind as the seat of intention and attention, something that can go away and be called back.
Shelter and defence asked of a god, the covering under which a household is safe.
The horse as draught animal, racer and sacrificial victim.
Food as sustenance and as what the gods are given, distinct from the oblation offered in the fire.
Deathlessness, the condition of the gods and the thing the sacrificer hopes the rite will extend to him.
The human adversary: rival, hostile tribe, or the Dasa and Dasyu the hymns set against the sacrificer.
The body or bodily person, what is protected, healed, or offered along with the offering.
The wind as a moving natural force, blowing, healing and driving the clouds.
Effective mental force: the capacity to form a plan and carry it out, attributed to gods and asked for by men.
The bull and the draught ox: the animal itself, and the same word used of a god whose strength is being praised, which the corpus does not distinguish.
The span of life granted or asked for, counted in autumns rather than lived as an abstraction.
The dwelling as a place and as the unit whose safety the rite secures.
The strewn grass on which the gods are invited to sit at the sacrifice.
Progeny and continuity of the line, one of the two things (with cattle) most often asked for.
The road travelled, literal and figurative, including the paths of order the gods keep to.
Stone as a substance and as ritual equipment: the pressing stones that crush the soma stalks, and stone generally as the hard thing a god splits or a press works with.
Melted butter, the commonest liquid oblation and a standing image for anything rich, streaming or nourishing.
A fixed observance or commandment, the particular rule as against the general order.
The sea or great gathered water, also used of the vat into which pressed soma streams.
Reverence offered in words and posture, the verbal accompaniment of an offering.
What is real and holds good, said of gods, of speech and of a promise.
The able man: the fighting son whose presence is itself counted among a household's goods.
Renown that outlasts a life, what a patron buys with liberality and a poet confers.
Armed conflict, from the raid for cattle to the set battle in which a god is asked to take a side.
The embryo or germ in the womb; the corpus applies the same word to the germ of fire in the waters, so this is the word's range and not only human pregnancy.
The day as a unit of time, and the days as the succession a life is counted in.
Giving as a virtue and as a transaction: the patron's gift, praised in the danastuti verses appended to many hymns.
Honey, and the honeyed quality attributed to soma, milk and speech alike.
Trees and the wood taken from them, including the sacrificial post and the forest as a place.
Darkness, both the night's and the hostile obscurity that light is asked to break.
Herbs and plants, addressed collectively and chiefly as healers.
The sung melody to which a verse is set, as distinct from the words of the verse.
The non-human hostile being -- rakshas, yatudhana, pishacha -- against whom whole Atharvavedic hymns are directed.
The space between heaven and earth, where wind, cloud and the Maruts move.
The dead forefathers as a class, receiving their own offerings and their own hymns.
The woollen filter through which the pressed soma is strained clean, and the purifying it performs.
Transformative craft, admirable in a god and treacherous in an enemy, with the same word for both.
Milk, both the cow's and the figurative milk of clouds, plants and the earth.
Wanting: the wish a rite is performed to fulfil, and in a few late hymns a cosmic first principle.
Birds, from the omen-bird of the Atharvaveda to the eagle that brings the soma down.
The wood with which the sacrificial fire is kindled, and the state of being kindled.
A mountain or rock mass, including the one Indra splits to free the cows and the waters.
The snake, both the animal charmed against in the Atharvaveda and the dragon Indra kills.
Fault or offence incurred against gods or men, thought of as something one is loosed from rather than forgiven for.
The man on whose behalf and at whose cost the rite is performed: not an officiant, and the party most of the corpus's requests are made for.
Gold, both as an object of wealth and as the colour of anything radiant.
The heart as the inward place where a hymn is formed and an intention is held.
Night as a division of time and as the interval the sacrificer asks to pass safely through.
The fee paid to the officiants, treated in the hymns as itself a meritorious act.
Weapons generally: bow, arrow and the gear a warrior or a god is armed with.
Thriving and increase asked for a household and its livestock, the fattening growth of what one already has rather than the acquisition of new goods.
Rainfall, asked for as the release of the waters held in the sky.
The officiant who does the physical work of the rite -- pressing, pouring, handling the vessels -- addressed in the plural as the men whose hands carry the offering.
Sheep, ewe and ram, and the fleece taken from them -- which is why this concept reaches Mandala 9, where the soma runs through a filter of sheep's wool.
Remedy and cure, the act of making whole, overwhelmingly an Atharvavedic concern.
The jar or pitcher into which the pressed soma runs and out of which it is drunk; the commonest vessel of Mandala 9.
The brahman as a person: the priest who holds the formulation, and the class of men who do. NOT the formulation itself, which is VG:CONCEPT:BRAHMAN-FORMULATION.
A world or region of space, including the free room a person is asked to be given.
The wild animal as against the herd animal: the deer or beast of the waste, hunted, snared, and used as the image of anything that roams.
The buffalo, dressed three hundred at a time in RV 5.29.7, and the same word applied to any bellowing power.
Lightning and thunder, the audible and visible violence of the storm.
Barley, the one cereal the corpus names constantly: ploughed, reaped, eaten, and offered, and the crop against which hunger is measured.

Amīvā: sickness in general, the affliction a god is asked to smite or expel rather than a named complaint. The one member of this group that is a four-Veda word -- Soma, Brahmaṇaspati and Vāstoṣpati are each called amīvahán, "slayer of amīvā".
Ploughed land and the work done on it, a small but distinct strand in the corpus.
Domestic animals taken together, the standing measure of a household's substance.
The wedding: the bride, the bridal procession that conveys her, and the marriage occasion itself.
Death as an event and as a power that binds, chiefly something to be kept away.

The cry uttered at the moment the oblation is released, svaha, and its counterpart the vasat-call. 326 passages carry it: 155 in the Yajurveda and 157 in the Atharvaveda against 14 in the Rigveda and none at all in the Samaveda, which makes it the sharpest sin

The pouring of the oblation into the fire, spoken as it is done: "juhomi", I pour (28 passages), and "juhota", pour ye (11). VS 7.26 puts the act, the caller's cry and the strainer in one line: "whatever drop of thine leaps forth, from the adhvaryu's hand or f
Poison as a substance in the body, whether from a snake, an insect, a plant or a poisoned arrow, and the thing charms declare to be sapless.

Yakṣma: the wasting, consuming sickness that is drawn out of a patient limb by limb in the Atharvaveda's ejection charms and flies away like a bird. Not fever, which is takman, and not affliction in general, which is amīvā.

The officiant who purifies, and the cup drawn from his station. The office is named at RV 2.1.2 and RV 1.94.6 (Griffith's "Cleanser", "Purifier"), the officiant sits down as potar at RV 4.9.3, and the Potar's cup is drunk from at RV 1.15.2, RV 2.36.2, RV 2.37.
The self or animating principle of a being, still concrete in this corpus and not yet the Upanishadic absolute.
Grain in general, and specifically the parched or roasted grain (dhānā) set out for Indra's horses and scattered for the dead.

Rapas: bodily hurt, blemish and defect -- the thing the wind is asked to blow away at AVS 4.13 and the thing Rudra is asked to carry one over at RV 2.33. Distinct from the root rap- "to prate", which is the same string in four other forms.
Heat generated by austerity, treated as a productive power rather than as self-denial.
The Turvaśas, the Yadus' constant pair; the one tribe name of this set that the Sāmaveda also carries.
Armour as a worn thing, literal mail and the figurative armour an amulet or a god is said to be; the object, not the shelter asked for.

The existent, what is, as against what is not. In this corpus still a substantivised neuter participle of as- 'to be' and not yet a settled noun: it is predicated of things and asked after, as in the one Being the sages call by many names (RV 1.164.46), and it

Imprecation and calumny, and the epithet abhiśastipā́ "protector against imprecation" that names it. Unlike the rest of this group it is not Atharvavedic property: 10 of its 18 token occurrences are Rigvedic or Yajurvedic.
The priest "placed in front" of a household or a king, an office the corpus attributes to men and to Agni in the same words.
The Pūrus, for whom Indra breaks open forts and makes room.
Trust that the rite and the god will hold good; in RV 10.151 a power addressed in its own right.
Metal, and specifically the dark metal the translators render "iron": the substance of Indra's bolt, of a fort, of a hook and of a blade.
Debt and the wish to be quit of it, owed to men, to the gods and to Death, and asked to be discharged rather than forgiven.
The offering ladle and spoon -- sruc, sruva -- with which butter is lifted and poured into the fire.

Varcas, the lustre a person is quickened with or bound into an amulet for; the Atharvaveda's commonest single request word after wellbeing. Only the instrumental and dative are aliases: the bare stem sits inside brāhmaṇavarcasá and hastivarcasá, which are othe
The excavated altar ground on which the grass is strewn and the offering set; in RV 1.164.35 the earth's own outermost limit.
The wish to put down a rival -- a competitor for rank, a rival claimant, a co-wife -- as distinct from defeating an enemy in war.
The noose or snare, above all Varuṇa's and Death's: the binding weapon a hymn asks to be released from rather than one it asks to be given.
The Yadus, named almost always in one breath with the Turvaśas as a distant people Indra brought or held back.

Non-existence: the asat of "there was neither non-existence nor existence then" (RV 10.129.1). Unlike sat it is already a noun in its own right -- the Rigvedic annotation lemmatises it asant-, separately from the root -- and existence is twice said to have spr
The drinking cup of the sacrifice, the one the Ṛbhus made fourfold and the one the gods are asked to drink from.
The Bharatas, the people for whom Agni is kindled in Mandala 3 and who ford the rivers in RV 3.33.

The officiant who leads or conducts, Griffith's "Leader", and the cup drawn from his station. The office at RV 2.1.2 and RV 10.91.10 ("tava neṣṭraṃ"), the cup at RV 1.15.9, RV 2.37.3 and RV 2.37.4, and in the Vajasaneyi Samhita at VS 26.22, "neṣṭrād ṛtubhir iṣ

Length of life, as the stated purpose of an act: the dative dīrghāyutvā́ya, "in order to length of life", is what an amulet is bound on for, what a patient is enclosed in red colours for, and what a husband is wished. That dative accounts for 15 of the entity'
The frog, whose croaking at the first rains is a whole hymn (RV 7.103) and a Yajurvedic sacrificial animal.
The moon, named chiefly where the corpus lists the lights of the sky together.

The second of the day's three soma pressings, named by its time of day at RV 3.28.4, RV 3.32.3, RV 5.40.4, AVS 7.76.6 and AVS 20.12.7, and by its ordinal at AVS 6.47.2 -- "asmin dvitīye savane", "at this second libation". VS 19.26 assigns it to Indra.
The wooden mortar and its pestle, the household pair that pounds grain and presses soma and is addressed as a divinity in RV 1.28.

The officiant who directs the rite, Griffith's "Director". Named as an agent at RV 1.94.6 ("praśāstā potā januṣā purohitaḥ") and RV 2.5.4 ("as Director was he born"), and as an office at RV 2.1.2 and RV 10.91.10 ("tava praśāstraṃ"). Agni holds it in all four.
Breath as the vital current, in the Atharvaveda already treated as the thing whose departure is death.
The goat: the victim led before the horse at the horse sacrifice, the animal cooked with five rice-dishes, and a head of ordinary livestock.
The war drum, addressed directly in the battle charms and told to roar the enemy away.

The first of the day's three soma pressings, named by its time of day. RV 3.28.1 and RV 3.52.4 offer the cake "prātaḥsāve"; AVS 6.47.1 has Agni protect us "prātaḥsavane"; and RV 10.112.1 calls it the first draught outright -- "prātaḥsāvas tava hi pūrvapītiḥ",
The axe or hatchet: the tool that fells the tree and the blade that jointed the sacrificial horse.
The Tṛtsus, Sudās's people in the battle of ten kings, confined to RV 7.18 and 7.83.
The yellow sickness, treated by transferring the patient's yellowness to yellow birds and taking the red of a bull in exchange.
The durnaman, "the ill-named": a class of noxious beings blamed for attacks on pregnant women and infants, distinct from the rakshas of the demon hymns.

The aśvatthá, the holy fig: born out of the khadira and told to crush the speaker's foes in AVS 3.6 and 8.8, named as the seat of the gods in the third heaven where they won the kuṣṭha, and the home of the herbs at RV 10.97.5.

The assembly and the gathering, "the two daughters of Prajāpati", as an occasion a man needs help at: to be favoured in, to be fit for, to speak what is pleasant in, and to have the witchcraft made against him there undone. sabhā́ and sámiti are folded togethe
The post to which the animal victim is tied, and the svaru splinter cut from it that is offered with the victim.

The officiant who kindles the fire. Two attestations, in two Vedas, and both were read: RV 2.1.2 and RV 10.91.10, where Agni is told "tvam agnid ṛtāyataḥ" (Griffith's "Kindler for the pious man"), and VS 7.15, where the kindler is addressed in the vocative at
The Vipāś, one of the two rivers Viśvāmitra addresses and asks to be forded in RV 3.33.
The Sarayu, named among the waters that might hold a traveller back.
The Yamunā, named in the river litany of RV 10.75 and among the allies of the Tṛtsus in RV 7.18.
Delivery as an occasion needing ritual help: the birth itself, the afterbirth, and the charm for causing conception.
The amulet: a bead, shell, plant or metal object bound on a person and addressed as the active agent of the charm.
The spoken curse -- a rival's, a sister's, a priest's in fury -- sent back to the curser rather than cured, and the thing an amulet or a herb is said to keep off.
Grahi, the Seizer: a seizing sickness personified as a female power whose fetters a patient is released from.

The khadirá, the hard-wooded acacia: the tree the aśvattha is born from, the wood of an amulet in AVS 10.6, one of the six trees the healing plant of AVS 5.5 arises from, and the timber a chariot axle is asked to be firm as at RV 3.53.19.
Agreement of mind within a household or an assembly, asked for as a positive good between kin and strangers alike.
The bowstring, addressed in its own right in the weapon hymns and the standing image for anything drawn taut.

The āñjana, the salve of the three-peaked mountain: addressed in the second person in AVS 4.9 and 19.44-45 as a protection that grinds up demons and sorceresses, told that fever, balāsa and the snake are its three slaves, and rubbed on by wives at a funeral. I
The dog: the household animal that is told to sleep in the two burglary charms, the hound that wakes the Ṛbhus, and one of the hundred gifts of a patron.
The student under the discipline of study and chastity, the subject of AVS 11.5 and of RV 10.109.5.
The disposal of the dead and the road they take: the cremation ground and the fathers' path, as against the ancestors themselves.
The Paruṣṇī, the river of the battle of ten kings, and in AVS 6.12 one of the streams said to run with honey.

The Sarasvatī as a place on the ground, on the only two occasions in the four Saṃhitās where the grammar says so: the barley the gods ploughed on it (AVS 6.30.1) and the rivers Agni is asked to shine on (RV 3.23.4). The goddess is VG:DEVATA:SARASVATI and is no
Darbha grass, addressed in its own hymns as an amulet that splits the heart of a rival; not the strewn barhis of the sacrifice.
The scorpion or stinger, slain with a club at AVS 10.4.9, ground up with the constrictor at 10.4.15, and told at RV 1.191.16 that its venom is weak.

The drawing and dedication of the soma draughts, cup by cup and deity by deity: the act the Vajasaneyi Samhita's seventh and eighth adhyayas are the formulary for, whose spoken words are "upayāmagṛhīto 'si" -- thou art taken with a support -- fifty-one times,

The priest who chants the Saman. Named exactly once in the four Samhitas, and in a simile: at RV 2.43.2 a bird is told "udgāteva śakune sāma gāyasi", "thou like the chanter-priest chantest the Sama". The Rigveda's manual annotation confirms the form as udgātár
The Ganges, named once in the river litany of RV 10.75 and nowhere else in the four Saṃhitās.
The Śutudrī, the Vipāś's companion in RV 3.33 and a name in the litany of RV 10.75.
